planting.note: Press fresh acorns an inch deep into loose, deep sand in fall; this clonal shrub oak needs well-drained, low-fertility dune sand and resents heavy or amended garden soil.

directions: Havard oak is the signature shrub of the deep sand dunes of the Llano Estacado and Chihuahuan Desert margins, including the Monahans Sandhills and Mescalero Sands, where its underground rhizomes send up dense, low thickets of lobed, leathery leaves known regionally as 'shinnery.' Because a single genetic individual can spread over acres by sprouting, it functions as an effective, nearly maintenance-free dune stabilizer and wildlife planting rather than a tidy specimen shrub. It is deciduous, coloring russet-bronze in fall, and its acorns are an important food source for scaled quail, turkey, and the lesser prairie-chicken. Give it full sun and loose, infertile sand; it has no tolerance for poor drainage or routine irrigation.

planting.note: Nick or hot-water-soak the hard-coated seed and direct sow in spring into loose, deep sand in full sun; this legume is a classic active-dune indicator and needs raw, shifting sand to perform, not garden loam.

directions: Dune broom is a sparsely leaved, gray-stemmed nitrogen-fixing shrub that specializes in the active, shifting sand dunes of the Chihuahuan, Sonoran, and Mojave deserts, including the dune fields around White Sands and the Monahans Sandhills. Its nearly leafless, finely haired stems reduce water loss on exposed dune crests, and in spring it produces short spikes of violet-purple pea flowers that draw native bees before the heat of summer. As a deep-rooted legume it fixes its own nitrogen and is valued in dune-restoration and xeriscape plantings for anchoring loose sand without irrigation or fertilizer. Avoid planting it in heavy or regularly watered soil, where it quickly declines.

planting.note: Direct sow or set small plugs in spring into gravelly, caliche, gypseous, or sandy soil in full sun; this woody-based mat is more broadly tolerant of mineral soil types than its narrow gypsum-endemic relatives and still needs sharp drainage.

directions: Woolly crinklemat forms a low, gray-woolly mat of small crinkled leaves across gypsum outcrops, caliche flats, and gravelly dune margins from West Texas through New Mexico and Arizona into northern Mexico, with small white-to-lavender flowers tucked close to the foliage through the warm months. Unlike its narrower gypsum-restricted relatives, it tolerates a wider range of raw mineral soils, which makes it a dependable choice for covering bare gravel or gypsum chips between boulders in a xeriscape or rock garden. It establishes slowly from seed or plugs and performs best left dry between infrequent rains. Overwatering or planting into rich, organic soil quickly causes crown rot.
